title: Sequitur
bodyHtml:
Space is valuable, so it's often desirable to compress data — that is, to use less space to convey the same information. One common data compression strategy is to identify repeated patterns within the data and somehow consolidate these repetitions.1 First, let's look at Sequitur, a fast compression algorithm that uses the repeated pattern strategy. The table below shows Sequitur running on the input “abcdbcabcd”, with its output at the very bottom:

If you want to know more about how linguists (and especially computational linguists) use compression in language technologies, try problem (I), Non Sequitur, in this booklet. Be aware, however, that solving problem (I) will not give you any advantage in solving this problem.

For each of the following inputs, say whether Sequitur and BPE give the same or different outputs.

hints.text: Compare how the two tables move. In the first table, Column 1 grows by exactly one symbol per step, so the algorithm is reading the input from left to right. In the second table, Column 1 starts as the whole input and gets rewritten all at once. Column 2 always lists the current string S plus every naming rule created so far.

Sequitur works online: as soon as some two-symbol pair occurs twice in the string built so far, it invents a new capital-letter name for that pair and replaces every occurrence, then keeps checking (a replacement can create a brand-new repeated pair, which must be named too). BPE works globally: it counts every two-symbol pair in the whole string, names the most frequent one (leftmost wins a tie), rewrites, and repeats. Because Sequitur reacts to the first repetition it meets and BPE reacts to the commonest one, the two can end up with unlike sets of rules.

Try the small input dede, which is not one of the graded items. Sequitur reads d, then de, then ded, then dede; at that point the pair de has occurred twice, so it names it, say W, and the string becomes WW with the rule W = de. BPE looks at dede as a whole: the pair de occurs twice, ed once, so it names de first and gets the same WW. Now notice why bigger inputs can split the two apart: whichever pair Sequitur happens to meet twice first need not be the pair that occurs most often overall.

explanationHtml:
What the tables are showing

Both algorithms compress a string by inventing short names for repeated chunks. A capital letter such as X is a nonterminal: it is not part of the data, it is a name that stands for a longer piece, defined by a rule like X = bc. Column 1 shows the string the algorithm is currently holding; Column 2 lists that string (as S = ...) together with every rule created so far.

How Sequitur works

Sequitur reads the input one symbol at a time, left to right. After each new symbol it asks: does any pair of adjacent symbols occur twice in what I am holding? If yes, it invents a new name for that pair and replaces all its occurrences; then it checks again, because a replacement can create a new repetition.

Follow the given input abcdbcabcd:

  • Steps 1 to 4 just add letters: a, ab, abc, and then the fourth letter d gives the string in Column 1 that matches S = abcd in Column 2. No pair repeats yet.
  • Step 5 adds b. Column 1 is abcdb, so Column 2 must simply record that string as S.
  • Step 6 adds c, giving abcdbc. Now the pair bc occurs twice (positions 2-3 and 5-6), so Sequitur names it X. Both copies are replaced, giving aXdX, and the rule X = bc is added. That is why step 6 has two rows.
  • Step 7 adds the next input letter a to aXdX. Column 1 becomes aXdXa. Its pairs are aX, Xd, dX, Xa - nothing repeats, so nothing is replaced, and Column 2 just repeats the string plus the rule already in force.
  • Step 8 adds b: aXdXab, still no repeated pair, so again the string is just recorded.
  • Step 9 adds c: aXdXabc. The letters bc at the end are exactly what X already stands for, so they are replaced: aXdXaX. But now the pair aX occurs twice, so a second nonterminal is needed: Y stands for aX, and both copies collapse. The string in Column 1 of the next row is therefore four symbols long, and Column 2 records it as S with the rules for X and Y.
  • Step 10 adds the last letter d. That makes the pair ending in d occur twice, so Sequitur names it Z and the string shrinks to ZXZ with Z = Yd.

Final output: S = ZXZ; X = bc; Y = aX; Z = Yd.

How BPE works

Byte Pair Encoding looks at the entire input at once. It counts every adjacent pair, replaces the commonest one everywhere (leftmost pair wins a tie), and repeats until no pair occurs more than once.

In abcdbcabcd the pairs are ab, bc, cd, db, bc, ca, ab, bc, cd. So bc wins with three occurrences: X = bc and the string becomes a seven-symbol string alternating a, X and d. In that string the pairs aX and Xd both occur twice, so the leftmost one, aX, is named Y, giving YdXYd - which is what the booklet already shows for step 3. There, Yd occurs twice, so Z = Yd and we finish at ZXZ. Same output as Sequitur, but reached in four steps instead of ten.

H3: when do they disagree?

The key difference: Sequitur reacts to the first repetition it bumps into while reading, BPE to the most frequent repetition in the whole string. When those are the same pair, the algorithms usually stay in step.

a) abcabdbcbc - Sequitur reads a, ab, abc, abca, abcab; at that moment ab has occurred twice, so it names ab first and continues, later naming bc. BPE counts the whole string and finds bc three times but ab only twice, so BPE names bc first. Different first choice, different final grammars: the outputs differ.

b) abbcaddca - the only pair that ever repeats is ca, and both algorithms find it, so the outputs match.

c) bacbcbabacbcba - Sequitur, reading left to right, meets cb as its first repetition, while BPE's global count picks ba first. From then on the two build different hierarchies, so the outputs differ.

d) ccdbccdbccacc - trace Sequitur: c, cc, ccd, ccdb, ccdbc, ccdbcc; now cc repeats, so X = cc and the string is XdbX. Adding d makes Xd repeat, so Y = Xd, giving YbY; adding b makes Yb repeat, so Z = Yb, giving ZZ. The remaining letters give ZZXaX. BPE's global counts pick cc first as well and it lands on the same grammar, so the outputs match.

e) ccdbccdbccaccacca - this is (d) with more repetition at the end, and now the tail changes which pair is commonest for BPE. Sequitur, still working left to right, keeps its earlier choices. The results end up structurally similar but built from different rules, so they count as different. (The official solution notes that because the two outputs differ only in which nonterminal symbols are used, the answer “Same” was given partial credit here.)

Why linguists care

Finding the repeated chunks of a string and naming them is very close to what a linguist does when discovering the words, prefixes and phrases of a language. Sequitur was designed to “identify hierarchical structure in sequences,” and BPE is used today to split text into subword units for language technologies.
